items.item: The CAP theorem states that in a network subject to communication failures, no web service can implement an atomic read/write shared memory that guarantees a response to every request.

at.step: Reveal: the theorem, in its own three exact conditions

items.item: Availability is a liveness property: every request to a non-failing node eventually receives a response.

at.step: Reveal: the theorem, in its own three exact conditions

items.item: The proof splits replicas into two groups with all messages between them lost; the minority group cannot distinguish a write having happened on the other side from nothing having happened, so it must refuse or risk answering incorrectly.

at.step: Reveal: the proof, on the shop's own register

items.item: A partition is not something a system chooses; the real choice CAP forces is consistency versus availability, made per operation during a partition, not declared once for the whole system.

at.step: Reveal: "pick two" is wrong, and why

items.item: Brewer's own words call the "2 of 3" formulation misleading because it oversimplified the tensions among the three properties.

at.step: Reveal: "pick two" is wrong, and why

items.item: PACELC adds an else-branch CAP says nothing about: even with no partition, a system still trades latency against consistency, because replicating before answering costs time.

at.step: Reveal: PACELC's else-branch

items.item: Dynamo-family systems are PA/EL, fully ACID systems are PC/EC, and PNUTS splits the two as PC/EL, each classified from the author's own quoted assignment.

items.item: Spanner's own architect states Spanner is technically a CP system, because partitions can and do happen at Google, and during some of them Spanner forfeits availability to keep consistency.

at.step: Reveal: Spanner is "effectively CA", not literally

items.item: Spanner is "effectively CA" only because partitions are rare enough on a private network that users can plan as if they do not occur, a statement about probability, not an exemption from the theorem.

at.step: Reveal: Spanner is "effectively CA", not literally

items.item: A system that has never yet experienced a partition is not exempt from CAP; the theorem constrains what a design must sacrifice if a partition occurs, independent of how often that has happened so far.

at.step: Prove it: a system that has never yet experienced a partition — does CAP apply?
